hero.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway to make way for mixed-use development in Vero Beach
hero.teaser: Crews began tearing down portions of the Indian River Mall this week as part of a revitalization project for the shopping center.
hero.body:
Crews began tearing down portions of the Indian River Mall this week as part of a revitalization project for the shopping center. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager working on the redevelopment project, said crews are working on the first phase, taking down the Macys and soon the former Sears location.

Neighbors gathered in the parking lot to watch the demolition. Mary Alice Stopyra said she is happy they are tearing it down because it has degraded over time. Mark Manera from Vero Beach said he has been coming to the mall for years and witnessed a steady decline year after year. Manera said change is needed and that if it brings new life, new jobs, and new opportunity, that would be wonderful.

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a new sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center, with around 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. Shoppers will not see a dead mall that was getting cobwebs for the last 12 years, he said, describing the project as a city within a city.

Scarfone said he hopes the first phase can be done by 2027. The team is still working on permitting for the rest of the project.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested after homeowner watches burglary unfold on security camera
cards.teaser: A Port St.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie man was arrested Thursday afternoon after a resident's home security camera caught him burglarizing an apartment in real time. Sebastian Thibodeau, 36, was charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling following the incident at Sanctuary Apartments at Winterlakes in the 5400 block of NW Moorehen Trail. The incident began around 3:38 p.m. when the apartment resident received a motion alert from his security system while away from home. Checking his live camera feed, he spotted a masked man inside his apartment. The resident activated his camera's audible siren, causing the suspect to leave briefly, only to return and tamper with the camera itself.

Multiple witnesses saw the suspect flee the victim's apartment and enter a neighboring unit in the same building. When Port St. Lucie Police arrived, they found clear signs of forced entry, including damage to the front door and door frame. Officers quickly established a perimeter while the SWAT team was called to assist. After repeated announcements, Thibodeau exited the apartment and surrendered without incident. Investigators collected surveillance footage from multiple sources throughout the complex, including doorbell cameras that captured a man matching the suspect's description before and after the burglary. Police found evidence that Thibodeau had attempted to obstruct security cameras and that a watch valued at approximately $300 was stolen during the burglary.

cards.headline: Florida Supreme Court adopts new AI courtroom rules after rampant misuse
cards.body:
Starting June 15, Florida attorneys and people representing themselves in court will need to verify and certify that everything they cite actually exists and is accurate. The Florida Supreme Court recently created new rules to address what legal experts and AI specialists widely recognize as a serious problem: artificial intelligence being misused in courtrooms. The consequences for breaking these rules can be significant, ranging from public reprimands to fines and even suspension from practicing law.

The problem has grown serious enough that Florida's highest court felt compelled to act. Federal Judge William Matthewman, who serves as chief magistrate for the Southern District of Florida, has dealt firsthand with AI misuse in his courtroom. "It's really a problem," he said, explaining that he believes things will likely get worse before they improve. "Unfortunately, I see it getting worse before it gets better. I think the Florida Supreme Court's order will help in Florida, but I unfortunately have seen over the last couple of years that it is growing and growing and growing," Matthewman said. He warned anyone filing court documents to ensure everything is accurate. "I would caution lawyers and parties representing themselves to make sure everything you file in court is accurate, because if not, you could find yourself in hot water," he said.

Recent cases illustrate the scope of the problem. In Polk County, a school district attorney filing a motion in a school bus camera lawsuit included fabricated facts and cited cases that don't exist. The attorney acknowledged using ChatGPT as a research tool but admitted there was no excuse for failing to verify the information before submitting it. The school district said it takes accuracy seriously and is reviewing whether the attorney can continue handling future work. Meanwhile, a St. Petersburg woman faced charges after using AI to create a fake photo of a man she claimed had burglarized and raped her. She later confessed the crime never happened.

Paul Figueroa, a Tampa criminal defense attorney who recently began using AI to streamline his work, emphasizes that the technology is unreliable. He described discovering that a quote AI provided, which seemed perfectly suited to his case, did not actually appear in the cited case. When asked if the new rules are sufficient, Figueroa said they are. "I do. I think it goes far enough for what we know now," he said. As courts work to manage AI's role in legal proceedings, the emphasis remains on human verification and accountability.

cards.headline: Florida weighs statewide fireworks ban ahead of July Fourth 250th anniversary
cards.body:
Florida state officials are closely monitoring drought conditions across the state as they consider whether to implement a statewide fireworks ban for Independence Day. The potential restriction would affect the 250th anniversary celebration of American independence. According to the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, this year's drought conditions are even more severe than those experienced in 1998, when Florida last imposed a statewide fireworks ban.

The drought situation has worsened significantly throughout Florida. Every part of the state is experiencing at least abnormally dry conditions, with certain regions facing particularly dire circumstances. Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast are among the areas dealing with moderate to extreme drought conditions. In May, Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson issued an early warning about the possibility of implementing a ban. Simpson emphasized the potential danger of the situation, explaining that if drought conditions persist, hundreds of thousands of people setting off fireworks in a single evening could ignite fires across the entire state simultaneously. Despite recognizing the historic importance of the 250th anniversary celebration, Simpson encouraged residents to explore alternative ways to mark the occasion.

Fireworks retailers have already noticed increased business activity from customers attempting to purchase supplies before any potential restrictions take effect. At Sky King Fireworks in West Palm Beach, staff reported a surge in customer traffic as residents shop ahead of the holiday. Bill Murphy, who works at the store, explained that they maintain careful monitoring of drought conditions to assess whether the ground has adequate moisture. However, Murphy expressed cautious optimism about this year's celebrations, noting that weather forecasts indicate significant rainfall is expected in the coming weeks.

The Florida Department of Agriculture has indicated that implementing a fireworks ban would represent a last resort measure. State officials will make their final determination about the ban as July Fourth approaches, basing their decision on how drought conditions develop over the coming weeks. The outcome will have widespread implications, potentially affecting both municipal fireworks displays and personal fireworks use throughout the state. As Florida residents anticipate one of the most significant Independence Day anniversaries in American history, they await the department's decision on whether traditional fireworks celebrations will be permitted this year.

cards.headline: Ocean could breach Jupiter Island at Peck Lake as erosion threatens to split island, state warns
cards.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report has documented severe erosion across nearly Jupiter Island's entire 11.5-mile coastline, raising concerns that the ocean could break through at Peck Lake and potentially split the island in half. The threat extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve, where private development faces immediate risk, to Peck Lake, where a breakthrough could convert a narrow strip of land into an open inlet. This area experienced a similar breach during a storm in the early 1960s, which the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers subsequently filled with sand. Mark Perry, with the Florida Oceanographic Society, warned that another breach could damage ecosystems that rely on specific balances between freshwater and saltwater. "We're going to probably have more storm surges that would create more of these breaks," Perry said. "That makes all these coastal marshes and everything vulnerable."

The erosion threatens far more than the physical landscape. Archaeological sites and wildlife refuges across the island face significant danger. The Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site, has already lost half its area to erosion. Conservation areas including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park are all at risk. Perry noted that over 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these areas. A separate state assessment identified additional concerns about mangrove swamps, which are critical for habitat and coastal protection, and warned that rising water levels could displace entire species from the island. "It's concerning because a lot of the conservation lands, and even historical and prehistorical sites, are at risk," Perry said.

Jupiter Island has been combating erosion through continuous maintenance efforts. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project that added enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. According to Commissioner Marshall Field, these ongoing efforts have prevented oceanfront homes from facing immediate danger. "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over," Field said. "We will continue to do that as long as there's money to do it." The town currently spends approximately $3 million annually in local taxpayer dollars on beach renourishment.

However, this funding remains uncertain. Field warned that a major breach could require substantial state and federal investment for repairs. "We would have cataclysmic erosion if we didn't get federal funding and state funding," he said. Field believes the recent FDEP assessment will help Jupiter Island compete more effectively for state and federal funding to address erosion. The fundamental challenge remains clear: maintaining the island requires consistent financial support that is far from guaranteed.

cards.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 1 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties
cards.teaser: Residents in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties must stop using fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen starting June 1 to reduce algae blooms during rainy season.
cards.body:
Starting June 1, residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties will no longer be able to use fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen on their lawns and landscaping. The restriction is designed to address a growing environmental concern during the region's rainy season, when nutrient-rich runoff flows into local waterways and can trigger harmful algae blooms.

According to Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, the ban targets a specific problem. When excess nutrients from fertilizers wash into water systems during heavy rains, they fuel the rapid growth of algae blooms that can threaten the health of ecosystems. Two major waterways in the region are particularly vulnerable to these blooms: the Indian River lagoon and the St. Lucie River. Skaggs explained that these blooms create multiple problems for aquatic environments. They can block out sunlight needed by beneficial plants that fish and wildlife depend on for food and habitat. In some cases, when algae blooms reach high densities, they produce toxins that can harm human health, damage wildlife populations, and degrade overall ecosystem quality.

The ban affects anyone maintaining outdoor spaces in these three counties, but experts point to practical alternatives. Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an effective substitute. Composting allows property owners to recycle organic waste while creating nutrient-rich material for their gardens and landscaping. Ricketts describes the process as straightforward and practical. A compost bin functions much like a small trash can where homeowners can deposit yard waste and other organic materials. Over time, these materials break down naturally and create a nutrient-dense amendment that can be worked into soil to support plant growth without the environmental risks associated with synthetic fertilizers.

For residents accustomed to using commercial fertilizer products, the transition may require adjusting their lawn care routines. However, the environmental benefits of the ban are significant. By reducing the flow of excess nutrients into waterways during Florida's wet season, the counties hope to prevent the algae blooms that have increasingly plagued the region's lagoons and rivers. Property owners who want to maintain healthy landscapes during the ban period should explore composting options or consult local extension services for additional guidance on alternative soil amendment methods.

Government officials across the Treasure Coast are assessing the impact of a property tax reform referendum set for November that would raise the homestead exemption. St. Lucie County faces $80 million in 2027-28 and $140 million in 2028-29. Indian River County faces $32 million in 2027-28 and $57 million in 2028-29. Powell noted that options like finding new revenue and budget cuts are possibilities if the measure passes, though the county has not yet determined whether this would mean increases in sales tax or user fees for other services. The referendum would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, a Republican from Stuart, said the proposal benefits struggling families in homes valued around $300,000.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island could see 9 feet of flooding at Emergency Operations Center
cards.teaser: A new vulnerability assessment by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection warns that Jupiter Island's Emergency Operations Center could see up to 9 feet of floodwater.

A funding application window opened June 1, and the town will take advantage of it. Field said evacuation orders would be issued well before floodwaters threaten roadways, and the town has a backup facility on the mainland to maintain operations during emergencies. The report warns that stormwater systems face some of the greatest risks, noting they can fail during the very flooding events they are designed to manage. Field acknowledged that improvements are needed, particularly along North Beach Road, but said the island's narrow, low-lying geography limits available solutions. Upgrading drainage infrastructure and transitioning from septic to sewer systems are among the town's top priorities.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance applications fill in hours as demand outpaces funding
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County receives nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month, but currently has only $2 million in combined grant funding for its Emergency Rental Assistance Program.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County's Emergency Rental Assistance Program, funded with nearly $2 million in combined grant funding, opens applications at the beginning of each month but faces overwhelming demand. According to program director Dr. James Green with the Community Services Department, the county typically receives about 600 applications within the first couple of hours of opening. Currently, approximately 800 applications are in the queue for rental assistance, and there are nearly 8,000 calls for housing assistance per month combined with 211 data. At the time of reporting, the county's assistance portal was marked closed due to high demand. Green said the demand far outweighs available resources, and the county is prioritizing those most in need. Anyone seeking assistance should call 1-833-CSD-WILL to check for availability.

The surge in applications reflects rising costs of living across housing, gas, and food. According to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Palm Beach County is $2,020 a month. Joanne Bromfield, who recently moved to West Palm Beach from Tampa after 12 years as an educator, switched to real estate to afford rent. Green emphasized the importance of keeping residents housed so they can continue working and supporting their families. For those unable to access the county program, 211 offers 24/7 connection to nonprofits and other assistance programs.

cards.headline: Florida shark dive operators fight federal feeding ban proposal
cards.teaser: A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast is drawing sharp criticism from the state's shark diving industry, with operators warning it could devastate conservation-driven tourism businesses.
cards.body:
The Safe Florida Seas Act, also known as H.R. 3831, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Supporters call it a common-sense safety measure to reduce human-shark interactions. However, shark diving operators say the bill unfairly targets their work while leaving fishing practices untouched. Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, noted that no one from Congress has asked dive operators to present data or explain their practices. Operators say they avoid surface chumming and instead take bait underwater during dives, which they argue is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food, unlike some commercial harvesting operations that release hundreds of gallons of chum at the surface.

Campbell points to Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving as a cautionary tale. Since that ban, shark incidents have increased and fatalities have been reported, according to industry members. The Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council found that at least one in four fishing trips ends with a shark biting off part of the catch. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Campbell is urging senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping any new rules.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island erosion could split island in half at Peck Lake, state report warns
cards.teaser: A state report found nearly the entire 11.5-mile shoreline of Jupiter Island is critically eroded, with the ocean threatening to break through at Peck Lake and potentially split the island in half.
cards.body:
The 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report found Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, potentially splitting the island in half. The threat stretches from Blowing Rocks Preserve, where private development is already at risk, to Peck Lake, where a breach could turn a thin strip of land into an open inlet. A storm breached Peck Lake in the early 1960s before the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers filled it back in with sand. Mark Perry with the Florida Oceanographic Society said a future breach could upend ecosystems that depend on a delicate balance of fresh and saltwater. A second state assessment warned erosion is also threatening mangrove swamps critical for habitat and coastal protection.

Among the sites at risk is the Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000 to 4,000-year-old archaeological site the report says is already half lost to erosion, along with Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park. Perry said there are over 33 threatened and endangered species in those areas. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the town continues to fight erosion through constant maintenance. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project, dumping enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Field said about $3 million in town taxpayer dollars goes toward beach renourishment every year.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County rental assistance program closes early each month as demand outpaces funding

cards.headline: Florida shark diving operators challenge federal feeding ban as bill clears U.S. House
cards.teaser: Emerald Charters owner Nathan Campbell and other Florida dive operators are pushing back against H.R. 3831, the Safe Florida Seas Act, which would ban shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida.
cards.body:
A federal proposal to ban shark feeding off Florida's coast has drawn sharp criticism from the state's shark diving industry. The measure, H.R. 3831 also known as the Safe Florida Seas Act, cleared the U.S. House and would prohibit shark feeding in federal waters within 200 miles of Florida, with an exception for harvesting. Supporters have called it a common-sense safety measure to reduce human-shark interactions. But a coalition of dive operators says the bill unfairly targets their work, often veteran-owned small businesses and nonprofits focused on education and conservation, while leaving fishing practices untouched.

Nathan Campbell, owner of Emerald Charters, said operators are requesting the chance to speak and share the science and facts, noting that no one from Congress has yet asked them to present data or explain their practices. The operators say they avoid surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives, which they argue is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats. The bill cites Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as precedent, but Campbell and some researchers say shark incidents actually increased in Hawaii after the ban. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Campbell is urging senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping any new rules.

hero.headline: Florida Supreme Court adopts new AI courtroom rules after rampant misuse
hero.body:
Starting June 15, Florida attorneys and people representing themselves in court will need to verify and certify that everything they cite actually exists and is accurate. The Florida Supreme Court recently created new rules to address what legal experts and AI specialists widely recognize as a serious problem: artificial intelligence being misused in courtrooms. The consequences for breaking these rules can be significant, ranging from public reprimands to fines and even suspension from practicing law.

The problem has grown serious enough that Florida's highest court felt compelled to act. Federal Judge William Matthewman, who serves as chief magistrate for the Southern District of Florida, has dealt firsthand with AI misuse in his courtroom. "It's really a problem," he said, explaining that he believes things will likely get worse before they improve. "Unfortunately, I see it getting worse before it gets better. I think the Florida Supreme Court's order will help in Florida, but I unfortunately have seen over the last couple of years that it is growing and growing and growing," Matthewman said. He warned anyone filing court documents to ensure everything is accurate. "I would caution lawyers and parties representing themselves to make sure everything you file in court is accurate, because if not, you could find yourself in hot water," he said.

Recent cases illustrate the scope of the problem. In Polk County, a school district attorney filing a motion in a school bus camera lawsuit included fabricated facts and cited cases that don't exist. The attorney acknowledged using ChatGPT as a research tool but admitted there was no excuse for failing to verify the information before submitting it. The school district said it takes accuracy seriously and is reviewing whether the attorney can continue handling future work. Meanwhile, a St. Petersburg woman faced charges after using AI to create a fake photo of a man she claimed had burglarized and raped her. She later confessed the crime never happened.

Paul Figueroa, a Tampa criminal defense attorney who recently began using AI to streamline his work, emphasizes that the technology is unreliable. He described discovering that a quote AI provided, which seemed perfectly suited to his case, did not actually appear in the cited case. When asked if the new rules are sufficient, Figueroa said they are. "I do. I think it goes far enough for what we know now," he said. As courts work to manage AI's role in legal proceedings, the emphasis remains on human verification and accountability.

cards.headline: Boca Raton pub draws soccer fans from Jupiter to Hollywood for World Cup matches

With America hosting the 2026 World Cup, Lion & Eagle is preparing for even larger crowds by adding extra bartenders, offering drink specials, and raffling off jerseys and tequila bottles to benefit the ARC of Palm Beach County. According to event founder Travis Suit, participants will launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13, arriving at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. All paddlers are required to wear a U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device, waterproof whistle, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times, and mandatory safety meetings will be held. Paddlers must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, while crew or virtual participants have a $500 minimum. Final contributions are due July 31. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 to cheer paddlers during a daylong beach celebration. More information and registration details are available at crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

He acknowledged that Venezuela ultimately needs multiparty, free, and fair elections to truly transition. Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Coral Gables Republican, also inquired about the timeline for change in Cuba, emphasizing that the Castro family continues to control the economy despite indictments.

Representative Lois Frankel, a West Palm Beach Democrat, raised concerns about administration pressure on the Gavi Alliance regarding international vaccine availability and disagreements with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy. Rubio disagreed with the characterization of Kennedy and clarified that the State Department, not the HHS Secretary, would oversee the Gavi Alliance moving forward. Representative Mario Díaz-Balart, a Hialeah Republican, urged Rubio to consider measures to limit China's influence in the Western Hemisphere. Rubio responded that American contractors need to be available to provide infrastructure as readily as Chinese competitors, noting this work has been a focus of embassies.

Operators distinguish their methods from commercial fishing by avoiding surface chumming, instead taking bait underwater during dives, which they argue is less likely to condition sharks to approach boats looking for food.

The bill cites Hawaii's 2006 ban on baited shark diving in federal waters as precedent, but Florida operators point to different results. Dr. Matt Ajemian, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University, says shark diving in Florida has a near perfect safety record for customers. Industry members note that since Hawaii's ban, shark incidents and fatalities have increased, and according to the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, at least one in four fishing trips ends with a shark biting off part of the catch. In a letter to Congress, Campbell is urging senators to delay action, gather research and involve all stakeholders in shaping any new rules.

hero.headline: Ocean could breach Jupiter Island at Peck Lake as erosion threatens to split island, state warns
hero.body:
A 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report has documented severe erosion across nearly Jupiter Island's entire 11.5-mile coastline, raising concerns that the ocean could break through at Peck Lake and potentially split the island in half. The threat extends from Blowing Rocks Preserve, where private development faces immediate risk, to Peck Lake, where a breakthrough could convert a narrow strip of land into an open inlet. This area experienced a similar breach during a storm in the early 1960s, which the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers subsequently filled with sand. Mark Perry, with the Florida Oceanographic Society, warned that another breach could damage ecosystems that rely on specific balances between freshwater and saltwater. "We're going to probably have more storm surges that would create more of these breaks," Perry said. "That makes all these coastal marshes and everything vulnerable."

The erosion threatens far more than the physical landscape. Archaeological sites and wildlife refuges across the island face significant danger. The Joseph Reed Mound, a 3,000- to 4,000-year-old archaeological site, has already lost half its area to erosion. Conservation areas including Blowing Rocks Preserve, Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge, and St Lucie Inlet Preserve State Park are all at risk. Perry noted that over 33 threatened and endangered species inhabit these areas. A separate state assessment identified additional concerns about mangrove swamps, which are critical for habitat and coastal protection, and warned that rising water levels could displace entire species from the island. "It's concerning because a lot of the conservation lands, and even historical and prehistorical sites, are at risk," Perry said.

Jupiter Island has been combating erosion through continuous maintenance efforts. In April 2025, the town completed a major beach renourishment project that added enough sand to fill nearly 400 Olympic-sized swimming pools. According to Commissioner Marshall Field, these ongoing efforts have prevented oceanfront homes from facing immediate danger. "We are just reapplying the Band-Aid over and over and over," Field said. "We will continue to do that as long as there's money to do it." The town currently spends approximately $3 million annually in local taxpayer dollars on beach renourishment.

However, this funding remains uncertain. Field warned that a major breach could require substantial state and federal investment for repairs. "We would have cataclysmic erosion if we didn't get federal funding and state funding," he said. Field believes the recent FDEP assessment will help Jupiter Island compete more effectively for state and federal funding to address erosion. The fundamental challenge remains clear: maintaining the island requires consistent financial support that is far from guaranteed.

hero.headline: Fertilizer ban begins June 1 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties
hero.teaser: Residents in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties must stop using fertilizer containing phosphorus or nitrogen starting June 1 to reduce algae blooms during rainy season.
hero.body:
Starting June 1, residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties will no longer be able to use fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen on their lawns and landscaping. The restriction is designed to address a growing environmental concern during the region's rainy season, when nutrient-rich runoff flows into local waterways and can trigger harmful algae blooms.

According to Jordan Skaggs with Environmental Resources in St. Lucie County, the ban targets a specific problem. When excess nutrients from fertilizers wash into water systems during heavy rains, they fuel the rapid growth of algae blooms that can threaten the health of ecosystems. Two major waterways in the region are particularly vulnerable to these blooms: the Indian River lagoon and the St. Lucie River. Skaggs explained that these blooms create multiple problems for aquatic environments. They can block out sunlight needed by beneficial plants that fish and wildlife depend on for food and habitat. In some cases, when algae blooms reach high densities, they produce toxins that can harm human health, damage wildlife populations, and degrade overall ecosystem quality.

The ban affects anyone maintaining outdoor spaces in these three counties, but experts point to practical alternatives. Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an effective substitute. Composting allows property owners to recycle organic waste while creating nutrient-rich material for their gardens and landscaping. Ricketts describes the process as straightforward and practical. A compost bin functions much like a small trash can where homeowners can deposit yard waste and other organic materials. Over time, these materials break down naturally and create a nutrient-dense amendment that can be worked into soil to support plant growth without the environmental risks associated with synthetic fertilizers.

For residents accustomed to using commercial fertilizer products, the transition may require adjusting their lawn care routines. However, the environmental benefits of the ban are significant. By reducing the flow of excess nutrients into waterways during Florida's wet season, the counties hope to prevent the algae blooms that have increasingly plagued the region's lagoons and rivers. Property owners who want to maintain healthy landscapes during the ban period should explore composting options or consult local extension services for additional guidance on alternative soil amendment methods.
